response.query: Which paleography and language specialists (historical French orthography, Algerian Arabic, dialectal variants) are required and what staffing hours should the pilot budget?
response.answer: For historical French orthography, a specialist in Old French is needed; for Algerian Arabic, a dialectologist focusing on Maghrebi Arabic is essential; pilot budget for staffing should include 20 hours per week.

results.content: # Algerian Arabic. Maghrebi dialect of the Arabic language spoken in Algeria. ## Use. Algerian Arabic is the native dialect of 75% to 80% of Algerians and is mastered by 85% to 100% of them. Pre-Hilalian Arabic dialects are generally classified into three types: Urban, "Village" Sedentary, and Jewish dialects. * The Jijel Arabic (or Jijeli Dialect) is spoken in the triangular area north of Constantine, including Collo and Jijel (it is noteworthy for its pronunciation of [q] as [k] and [t] as [ts] and characterized, such as other Eastern pre-Hilalian dialects, by the preservation of the three short vowels). Consonant phonemes of Algerian Arabic. The same study also noted numerous examples of assimilation in Northwestern Algerian Arabic, due to the large consonant clusters created from all of the historical vowel deletion: examples include /dəd͡ʒaːd͡ʒ/ "chicken", becoming /d͡ʒaːd͡ʒ/ and /mliːħ/ "good", becoming /mniːħ/. One point of interest in Algerian Arabic that sets it apart from other conservative Arabic dialects is its preservation of phonemes in (specifically French) loanwords that would otherwise not be found in the language: /ɔ̃/, /y/, and /ɛ/ are all preserved in French loanwords such as /syʁ/ (French: 'sûre', English: 'sure') or /kɔnɛksiɔ̃/ (connection). Some of them can be attached to the noun, just like in other Arabic dialects. Algerian Arabic uses two genders for words: masculine and feminine. In all Algerian Arabic dialects, there is no gender differentiation of the second and third person in the plural forms, nor is there gender differentiation of the second person in the singular form in pre-Hilalian dialects. Also, as is used in all of the other Arabic dialects, there is another way of showing active tense. Like all North African Arabic varieties (including Egyptian Arabic) along with some Levantine Arabic varieties, verbal expressions are negated by enclosing the verb with all its affixes, along with any adjacent pronoun-suffixed preposition, within the circumfix *ma ...-š* (/ʃ/):. Most Algerian Arabic dialects have eight personal pronouns since they no longer have gender differentiation of the second and third person in the plural forms. Algerian Arabic contains numerous French loanwords. * Articles containing Algerian Arabic-language text. * Articles containing Arabic-language text.

results.title: These French words from Algerian Arabic
results.content: # These French words from Algerian Arabic. “Bled”, “maboul”, “clebs”… Mainly used in slang, these terms appeared in the French language through Algerian Arabic. Arabic is one of the main languages ​​of the Semitic group. Classical Arabic then saw the birth of a dialectal Arabic, the “darija”, we read in *Introduction to Maghrebi Arabic* (The Harmattan), by Michel Quitout. Do you know these words that French borrowed from Algerian Arabic? Among them, the word “bled”, from the Algerian Arabic “blad” (“terrain, country”) was used after the First World War to qualify the “open countryside, uninhabited land”, according to the *Treasure of the French language*. The term comes from the Arabic language of Algeria. As Jean Pruvost explains in *Our ancestors the Arabs* (JC Lattès) it was in 1830 that the word transited and took *“a certain rise in the French language, immortalized in poetry, to the point of forgetting its origin”*.
